briefing.opening: Good day. We begin the Climate Change Daily Briefing for November 25, 2026.

sections.title: 🌍 COP31 Climate Talks Collapse Amid Diplomatic Impasse
sections.content: The 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, collapsed without reaching a final agreement due to sharp divisions over fossil fuels, among other issues [90, 95, 108]. Key sectoral agreements—including those on food, forests, oceans, and nature—also fell through, with scenes of confusion and panic observed among key figures such as COP President and Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen [108, 110]. While some express hope for the emergence of new climate coalitions and an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels, growing concerns remain that the absence of a final agreement could weaken climate resilience signals for vulnerable areas, including major tourist destinations [103, 104].

sections.title: ⚠️ Extreme Weather Disasters Accelerate Crises Across Ecosystems and Infrastructure
sections.content: Driven by climate change and El Niño, aviation weather hazards such as severe turbulence and aircraft icing are becoming more frequent and unpredictable, disrupting flight safety operations [2, 96]. Additionally, atmospheric moisture and stagnation have significantly intensified the frequency and severity of extreme rainfall, leaving the vast majority of homes exposed and vulnerable to flood risks, as witnessed in the downtown flooding of San Francisco, California [10, 16, 17, 92]. Cumulative damage is also mounting across ecosystems and primary industries: over 10,000 sea lions have died in Peru, while in South Korea, abnormal heatwaves and droughts have caused rice yields in key production areas of Jeonbuk to plummet by over 30% [3, 83].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Current Status of Domestic Renewable Energy Deployment and Challenges in the Power Market
sections.content: Although South Korea's electricity market has taken its first steps toward a carbon-neutral contract market, domestic renewable energy generation accounted for only 9.8% of the power mix last year—falling short of targets—while concerns have surfaced regarding disruptions to public deliberation on nuclear energy [47, 70, 73]. Concurrently, amid intense global deployment competition, a crisis in the domestic solar manufacturing sector has been highlighted, prompting calls to link deployment policies with domestic manufacturing support [66]. In response, the Korea Power Exchange (KPX) is seeking structural market reforms to accommodate renewable energy expansion, while local councils in Gyeonggi-do and Busan are demanding tangible emissions reductions and citizen-focused budget execution [38, 49, 69, 74].

sections.title: 🌱 Local Governments and Industry Drive Regional Carbon Neutrality Initiatives
sections.content: Efforts to build renewable energy infrastructure at the municipal level remain active, with Dangjin City selected for the 2027 Renewable Energy Convergence Support Project and Seo-gu, Daegu investing over 200 million won to expand solar deployment [59, 60]. Institutions such as the Incheon Institute have emphasized the necessity of everyday citizen participation and lifestyle-benefit policies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045, while Cheongyang County is operating 'Carbon-Upshu,' a climate-action financial incentive program [40, 46, 56]. Furthermore, in the retail and food sectors, initiatives such as the 'Tomorrow's Farm' brand—powered by advanced smart farm technologies—are successfully securing fresh food supply chains in the face of climate change [4, 7, 20].

briefing.closing: Despite the diplomatic impasse in the international community, on-the-ground technology adoption and localized actions to address the climate crisis continue. That concludes today's climate briefing.
